decisions.evidence: Presentation round 3: “paste any link… Get details… Save bookmark.” Client round 3: “A big box… to drop a link into… exactly… the start I was hoping for.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: saving begins by entering a URL, conforming to the reference.

decisions.evidence: Presentation round 3: “fetched title, description, icon, and preview.” Client round 3 confirms it “pulls up the page’s picture, its icon… title and description.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: automatic metadata collection covers all required fields.

decisions.evidence: Presentation rounds 3–6: fetched title and description appear “for review before saving”; round 6 summarizes “reviewing and editing fetched details.” Client rounds 3 and 6 explicitly approves editing them.
decisions.note: Prototype review: collected title and description are editable in the save flow; later presentations retain general editing.

decisions.evidence: Presentation round 4 defines the card as showing “picture, site identity, title, and description,” omitting tags. Client round 4 approves that exact composition: “picture… icon and name, the title, and the description all on it.”
decisions.note: Early prototype review: the explicitly presented card composition omitted the reference-required tags; the response approved it without identifying the omission. A later tag prototype revised the presentation.

decisions.evidence: Presentation round 5: selecting the saved card’s title “should reopen the original page in a new browser tab.” Client round 5: “that’s the natural way.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: making the title the opening control is functionally equivalent to selecting the item.

decisions.evidence: Revised presentation round 7 shows tagged cards; client round 7 observes that “the reading one [was] also tagged ‘work.’” Round 33 presents consistently sized readable cards with full content on the details view; client round 34 approves.
decisions.note: Later prototype review: the revised cards expose tags and retain readable title/description previews, resolving the earlier card-composition omission.

decisions.evidence: Presentation round 7: “bookmarks may carry more than one tag.” Client round 7 approves and notes a bookmark carrying both reading and work tags.
decisions.note: Prototype review: assigning multiple tags conforms to the reference.

decisions.evidence: Presentation round 7 asks the client to select Recipes and see only recipe cards with the active tag visible. Client round 7 confirms exactly that result.
decisions.note: Prototype review: selecting one tag filters the collection to that tag.

decisions.evidence: Presentation round 8 offers A, manual tag entry; B, a fixed set; and C, existing selectable tags plus creation of a new tag. Client round 8 selects C because it lets her “pick from what I’ve got, or type a new one,” rejecting A’s lack of existing-tag suggestions and B’s fixed-only limitation.
decisions.note: Prototype choice: the alternatives differed in reference fulfillment, and the client selected the reference-conforming interaction. A selectable list of existing tags is functionally equivalent to autocomplete here.

decisions.evidence: Presentation rounds 8–11 supports changing tags and notes while editing an existing bookmark. Client rounds 9 and 11 approves adding/creating tags and editing the bookmark-specific note later.
decisions.note: Prototype review: post-save editing of tags and notes conforms for those fields; URL editing is assessed separately at the specification gate.

decisions.evidence: Presentation rounds 10–11 defines the complete note behavior as entering a short note, displaying it in a “Your note” block, and editing it later; no Markdown authoring or rendering is presented. Client round 11 approves these as “all” the note behaviors. Round 39 retains only “personal notes” in the approved scope.
decisions.note: Prototype/specification review: notes are supported, but the settled behavior omits the reference-required Markdown rendering. The client does not surface that difference.

decisions.evidence: Presentation rounds 12–14 tests uppercase CONFERENCE and COMFORTING against lowercase note/description text. Client confirms both match regardless of capitalization.
decisions.note: Prototype review: search is explicitly case-insensitive.

decisions.evidence: Presentation rounds 13–14 calls the completed search scope “titles, descriptions, and notes”; URL is omitted. Client round 14 repeats and approves that exact field set without mentioning URL.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the finalized full-text search decision omits URL search, so it only partially fulfills REF-BM-12.

decisions.evidence: Presentation round 14 declares “all the search behaviors we checked” to be live filtering over titles, descriptions, and notes; no #tag syntax is included. Client round 14 approves this as “the search I wanted.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: the settled search behavior omits #tag search, and the response does not identify the omission.

decisions.evidence: Presentation rounds 13–14 treats basic text matching as completing the search behavior and includes no AND/OR/NOT operators or parenthesized groups. Client approves without raising advanced Boolean search.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the settled search behavior omits the reference Boolean grammar.

decisions.evidence: Presentation round 14 exhaustively summarizes the checked search behavior without exact quoted-phrase matching. Client round 14 accepts the summary without identifying that difference.
decisions.note: Prototype review: exact quoted-phrase search is absent from the settled search decision.

decisions.evidence: Presentation round 15 offers three controls that mark a card Read later. Client selects A, the explicit “Read later” button, and confirms that it changes to “In Read later.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: all offered controls perform the required unread/read-later marking; the preference among them is orthogonal.

decisions.evidence: Presentation round 16: selecting Read later produces a focused list of waiting items. Client round 16 confirms it “narrowed down to just the things I’d set aside to read.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: a separate unread-only view conforms.

decisions.evidence: Presentation rounds 16–17 changes the action to “Mark as read” and removes the item from Read later while retaining it in the collection. Client round 17 explicitly approves; rounds 29–30 confirm the last item behaves the same way.
decisions.note: Prototype review: marking as read removes an item only from the unread list.

decisions.evidence: Presentation rounds 18–19 detects a submitted duplicate before another save, keeps the count unchanged, and opens the existing bookmark with edit/open actions. Client round 19 says this is “exactly what I wanted.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: directing the user to the existing bookmark with an explicit edit action is functionally equivalent to guiding them to edit it.

decisions.evidence: Presentation round 20 removes an archived bookmark from the main collection and increases the Archive count. Client selects the direct Archive button and confirms the behavior.
decisions.note: Prototype review: archive hides an item from the default collection while retaining it.

decisions.evidence: Presentation round 21 opens Archive, finds the retained bookmark, and offers “Restore to collection.” Client confirms the archived item appears there with all details intact.
decisions.note: Prototype review: a separate archive list is provided.

decisions.evidence: Presentation rounds 21–22 makes archive reversible through “Restore to collection.” Client round 21 explicitly characterizes this as “different from deleting for good.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: the archive behavior is explicitly understood as reversible and conceptually distinct from permanent deletion; the missing delete operation itself is assessed under REF-BM-05.

decisions.evidence: Presentation rounds 31–32 blocks submission of a non-web-address value, leaves the count unchanged, and keeps the field ready for correction. Client approves the behavior.
decisions.note: Prototype review: enforcing the requirement that the saved value be a URL conforms; the particular validation presentation is otherwise an orthogonal UX choice.

decisions.evidence: Presentation rounds 33–34 shortens unusually long card previews for scanning while retaining full title and description on the details view. Client approves this tradeoff.
decisions.note: Prototype review: shortened but visible previews are a readability-first, functionally equivalent presentation.

decisions.evidence: Presentation rounds 35–36 proposes trimming spaces and ignoring capitalization so ` Reading ` reuses `reading`. Client says this prevents near-duplicate tags and keeps bookmarks under one tag.
decisions.note: Prototype review: tag normalization supports the unique-tag constraint and does not conflict with tag assignment or reuse.

decisions.evidence: Specification gate round 39 exhaustively lists the approved editing scope as enriched details, tags, and personal notes, after prototypes only demonstrated title/description editing before save and tag/note editing afterward; editing a saved bookmark’s URL is never included. Client round 39 says the listed scope “covers everything.”
decisions.note: Specification gate: saved-URL editing is missing from the approved implementation scope, and the client does not identify the omission.

decisions.evidence: Specification gate round 39 lists archive and restore but no permanent delete operation. Client round 39 approves the listed scope as complete; implementation review round 40 again names archive/restore without delete and is accepted.
decisions.note: Specification gate, reiterated at implementation review: permanent bookmark deletion is omitted without an explicit client response to that difference.

decisions.evidence: Specification gate round 39 calls the 15 listed flows the approved scope, but includes no multi-selection or bulk add/remove tags, read/unread, archive, or delete actions. Client approves the scope without mentioning bulk actions.
decisions.note: Specification gate: multi-bookmark bulk actions are omitted.

decisions.evidence: Specification gate round 39 includes filtering and collection handling but no action applied to the whole currently filtered collection. Client round 39 approves the listed scope as covering everything hoped for.
decisions.note: Specification gate: whole-filter bulk actions are omitted independently of ordinary multi-selection.

decisions.evidence: Rounds 33–34 settle large-collection handling through shortened cards, search, counts, and filters, with no sorting control. Round 39’s complete approved scope likewise omits sorting; the client approves it.
decisions.note: Specification gate: list sorting is absent from the approved large-collection behavior.

decisions.evidence: Presentation rounds 37–38 defines preservation as retaining title, description, picture, notes, and tags while the original link opens current content; it never presents a stored HTML/PDF snapshot. Round 39 includes only “preservation of saved details over time.” Client approves without mentioning an original-page snapshot.
decisions.note: Prototype/specification gate: preservation is limited to bookmark metadata rather than a local single-file HTML snapshot or stored PDF. The client does not explicitly identify or accept that difference.

decisions.evidence: Specification gate round 39 presents the complete approved scope without Internet Archive snapshot creation. Client round 39 approves that scope without raising this capability.
decisions.note: Specification gate: Internet Archive snapshot support is omitted.

decisions.evidence: Specification gate round 39 includes ordinary search and tag filtering but no reusable bundle combining a search term with included/excluded tags. Client approves the listed scope as complete.
decisions.note: Specification gate: saved dynamic filter bundles are omitted.

decisions.evidence: Specification gate round 39’s complete feature-flow list contains no Netscape HTML import. Client round 39 approves the scope without mentioning import.
decisions.note: Specification gate: bookmark import is omitted.

decisions.evidence: Specification gate round 39’s complete feature-flow list contains no Netscape HTML export. Client round 39 approves the scope without mentioning export.
decisions.note: Specification gate: bookmark export is omitted independently of import.

decisions.evidence: Specification gate round 39 presents the complete approved scope without profile settings for default sort, displayed items, or font size. Client approves the listed scope as covering everything hoped for.
decisions.note: Specification gate: display-related personal settings are omitted.
